newsitem.title: UK: Time for hard look at UK energy regulators - Eggar.
newsitem.headline: Time for hard look at UK energy regulators - Eggar.

text.p: Former energy minister Tim Eggar said on Wednesday that the regulators of Britain's gas and electricity industries should be made accountable to a new parliamentary Select Committee on Regulated Industries.
The proposal was one of several suggestions Eggar made for improving the effectiveness and accountability of the regulators, who enjoy statutory independence from ministers.

"Parliament has given the regulators considerable powers and independence. The time has arrived for a thorough, considered and objective look at their role," Eggar told parliament's Trade and Industry Committee.
Eggar said creating a specialist select committee that would develop expertise in regulation would help to remedy what he called a "democratic deficit" in the current system.
Eggar, who stepped down as energy minister in July, said the practical arguments currently for separate gas and electricty regulators were compelling.
But he said once supply competition was firmly embedded by 2000-2002, only the common carrier distribution systems would need regulation and that could be done by one Energy Regulator.

Eggar also called for more clarity in the interaction between regulation and general competition law and suggested allowing a right of appeal to the Mergers and Monopolies Commission by consumer panels or named consumer groups.
Even individuals might be allowed to appeal through a sifting system run by the Office of Fair Trading.
Eggar listed five areas where the methodology and quality of decision-taking by the regulators could be improved:

-- transparency. Although the ultimate decision on price-setting is bound to be a matter of confidential judgement, regulated companies should consider whether the information they provide to the regulator needs to be kept confidential.
-- Ofgas and Offer should improve current "haphazard" consumer consultation procedures.
-- Eggar rejected the idea of a panel of regulators but said individual regulators should appoint boards of advisors, rather like non-executive directors.

-- He defended the RPI-x pricing formula, noting most countries introducing regulatory systems are choosing this basic approach rather than a rate of return system, but said it should put a heavy emphasis on incentives for cost reduction.
-- the director generals of the regulatory offices should be allowed to recruit a small number of specialists on short-term assignments and pay them well above civil service grades.
